readerTitle: The customers who give up before they buy
caseNote: 가상 사례 (포장재 제조사의 재주문 과정, 경비 정산 앱) · 일상 장면은 일반적인 경험 묘사
insight: 고객을 잃는 순간은 '거절'이 아니라 '나중에 하지'다. 원하는 것과 실제 행동 사이의 단계·대기·불확실성을 하나씩 줄이면 가격을 건드리지 않고도 행동이 늘어난다.
misconception: 고객이 사지 않거나 다시 주문하지 않는 이유는 가격이나 제품이 마음에 들지 않아서다. 단계 하나쯤 더 있는 건 큰 문제가 아니다.

sources.text: 행동경제학의 일반 개념 (마찰, 'make it easy' 원칙). 배경 자료: Thaler, R. & Sunstein, C. (2008). Nudge. Yale University Press.

cards.title: The customers who give up before they buy
body: You meant to book that dentist appointment. Then the phone line opened at 9, you were in a meeting, and it slid to next week.
You didn't decide against the dentist. You just never got around to it. Your customers do the same thing to you, and they almost never tell you.

image.label: A to-do note with one task carried over day after day
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 냉장고에 붙은 포스트잇 한 장 "Book dentist"가 월·화·수·목 달력 칸으로 계속 밀려 옮겨지는 모습. 따뜻하고 약간 유머러스한 톤. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your best customers are reordering less.
body: You make shipping boxes. Your warehouse customers like your quality and your prices are fair. But reorders have slowed, and some customers now go weeks between orders.
To reorder, a customer emails for a quote, waits for a reply, signs a PDF and sends a purchase order. What do you try first?

options.text: Cut prices by 5% for repeat orders
options.feedback: It costs you margin on every order, and it fixes a problem customers may not have. If the quote still takes a day, the reorder still waits in someone's inbox.

options.text: Let customers repeat a past order in one step, with the price shown up front
options.feedback: You keep your price and remove the waiting and paperwork between "we need boxes" and "ordered". It takes setup work, but it works on every order after that.

options.text: Have a sales rep call each customer every month
options.feedback: The calls catch some orders that would have slipped. But they add cost for you and an interruption for them, and the slow process behind the call stays the same.

cards.title: Follow one reorder.
body: None of these steps is hard. Together they turn "I'll order now" into "I'll do it later". Meanwhile, a rival let buyers reorder online in about two minutes, and **later** often became *never*.

breakdown.label: Email for a quote
breakdown.detail: The buyer notices stock is low, between ten other tasks

breakdown.label: Quote arrives
breakdown.detail: Now there's a PDF to print, sign and scan

breakdown.label: Purchase order
breakdown.detail: Needs a manager's approval, who is travelling

breakdown.label: Order placed, maybe
breakdown.detail: Or the buyer tried the rival's site instead

cards.title: Friction
body: **Friction** is anything that stands between wanting to do something and actually doing it: extra steps, waiting, missing information, or effort spent thinking.
The key point: friction rarely makes people say no. It makes them say *not now*. And every "not now" is a chance for something else to win their attention, or for the need to fade.

image.label: A path from 'want' to 'done' with small obstacles along it
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Want"에서 오른쪽 "Done"으로 가는 길 위에 작은 장애물 4개: 계단(Steps), 모래시계(Waiting), 물음표(Unknowns), 뇌 아이콘(Thinking). 길 중간에서 옆길로 빠지는 점선 화살표에 "Not now" 라벨.

cards.title: Four kinds of friction to look for.
body: When customers stall, the cause is usually one of these:
list: **Steps:** every form field, click, signature or trip adds a place to stop
**Waiting:** a reply tomorrow loses to an answer now
**Unknowns:** no price shown, unclear delivery date, "what happens next?"
**Thinking:** choices the customer must work out alone, like codes, sizes or specs
cards.callout: Small frictions add up. Removing one rarely feels dramatic, but removing several can change behavior.
cards.softwareNote: In software, friction hides in logins that expire, settings people must find, and screens that ask for information you already have. Each one is a place where users drift away quietly.

cards.title: Friction is a tool, not just a flaw.
body: Friction works both ways. Remove it from what you *want* customers to do. Add a little where a mistake would be costly.
A wholesaler might add a confirmation step before an unusually large order ships. A bank asks you to confirm a big transfer. That pause protects the customer, and it builds trust.
The skill is choosing where friction goes, instead of letting it pile up by accident.

cards.title: Not all friction should go.
body: Some steps carry real value: a credit check, a safety question, a measurement that prevents the wrong part being shipped. Cut those and you trade fewer drop-offs for more errors and returns.
Making it hard to *leave* is also friction, and customers notice. It may keep some for a while, but it costs you trust and goodwill.
And don't guess. Look at where people actually stop before deciding which step to remove.

cards.title: Now it's an expense app.
body: Your app helps companies collect employee receipts. Finance teams love it, but employees submit receipts late, often weeks after a trip. Each receipt needs a photo upload on a laptop, then five fields typed by hand.

options.text: Send more reminder emails to late employees
options.feedback: Reminders bring some people back, but each one still lands on the same slow laptop process. You raise the nagging without lowering the effort.

options.text: Let employees snap the receipt on their phone, with fields filled in for them to check
options.feedback: It removes the trip to the laptop and most of the typing, right when the receipt is in their hand. The cost is building and checking the auto-fill.

options.text: Add a required project code so finance gets better data
options.feedback: Finance gains cleaner reports, but employees face one more thing to look up. Submissions could get even later, which hurts the finance team too.

cards.title: Customers rarely say no. They say not now.
body: Before cutting prices or adding reminders, count the steps, waits and unknowns between wanting and doing. Remove what doesn't protect the customer.
**Try it today:** buy, book or reorder from your own business as a customer would. Write down every moment you had to wait, type, guess or ask.
